description:
Operational dashboard for the CyberChef MCP server (v2.7.0+).

Every panel except the Latency row works against the built-in, dependency-free /metrics endpoint alone. The Latency row additionally needs an OpenTelemetry SDK, which the operator supplies -- see deploy/grafana/README.md.

links.title: Metric reference
links.tooltip: What each series means, and what is deliberately not exposed

panels.title: Serving
panels.description: Replicas reporting the `serving` lifecycle state. A draining replica is excluded here but is still finishing in-flight work -- the state timeline below shows both at once.

panels.title: Draining
panels.description:
Replicas that received SIGTERM and are refusing new traffic while finishing in-flight requests.

Non-zero during a rolling update is CORRECT. Non-zero for longer than `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` means a drain is stuck and the kubelet will SIGKILL it.

panels.title: Operations / sec
panels.description: Operations accepted by the quota tracker, across the selection. Counts every operation the server started, including those that later failed.

panels.title: Tool failure rate
panels.description:
Failed tool executions as a fraction of all tool executions.

Derived from monotonic counters, so this is a true rate. An earlier draft derived it from the telemetry ring buffer, which drops its oldest entries -- Prometheus reads a falling counter as a restart, so `rate()` over it invents traffic that never happened.

panels.title: Cache hit ratio
panels.description: Tool executions served from the operation cache. The cache is per-process, so with several replicas this is an average across them, and a rollout resets it to zero.

panels.title: Version
panels.description: From `cyberchef_mcp_build_info`. More than one value here means a rollout is in progress -- or that one stalled part-way, which is worth checking against the deployment.

panels.title: Shortest uptime
panels.description: Minimum uptime across the selection. A drop is a restart; the purple annotations mark each one. Correlate with Draining to tell a planned roll from a crash.

panels.title: Lifecycle state per replica
panels.description:
The three lifecycle states over time, one row per replica.

This is the panel to read during a deploy. A correct rolling update looks like a band of `draining` that appears on one replica at a time and disappears within the drain budget, while at least one other replica stays `serving` throughout.

Two shapes are faults: `draining` that never ends (the drain is stuck and will be SIGKILLed), and every replica leaving `serving` at once (the update had no surge capacity, and traffic was dropped).

`starting` should be a sliver -- cold start is ~185 ms since v2.6.0.

panels.title: Tool call rate (top 10)
panels.description:
Which tools are actually being used.

Sourced from monotonic counters that are maintained whether or not per-call telemetry buffering is enabled, so this is populated on a DEFAULT deployment. `CYBERCHEF_TELEMETRY_ENABLED` gates the per-call records (durations, sizes, timestamps), not the fact that a tool ran.

panels.title: Call volume by tool
panels.description:
Total executions in the selected window, ranked.

A companion to the rate graph beside it, and a better answer to "what is this server actually FOR": with 300+ tools registered, real deployments use a handful heavily and the rest never. That distribution is the argument for the curated tool surface -- the default set should be the left-hand end of this chart.

panels.title: Failure rate by tool (top 10)
panels.description:
Failures per second by tool.

Read the SHAPE against the call-rate panel: failures tracking calls proportionally is usually bad input from one caller; failures flat while calls climb is usually a limit being hit -- check the rate limiter and quota panels below.

panels.title: Tool leaderboard
panels.description:
Call rate, failure rate and cache hit ratio per tool, joined into one row each.

Sorted by call rate. The failure-rate column is coloured against the same thresholds as the headline stat (1% amber, 5% red), so a tool misbehaving inside otherwise-healthy aggregate traffic is visible here rather than being averaged away above.

Click a tool name to filter the whole dashboard to it.

targets.expr: sum by (tool) (rate(cyberchef_mcp_tool_failures_total{job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance", tool=~"$tool"}[$__rate_interval])) / clamp_min(sum by (tool) (rate(cyberchef_mcp_tool_calls_total{job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance", tool=~"$tool"}[$__rate_interval])), 1e-9)

sum by (tool) (rate(cyberchef_mcp_tool_cache_hits_total{job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance", tool=~"$tool"}[$__rate_interval])) / clamp_min(sum by (tool) (rate(cyberchef_mcp_tool_calls_total{job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance", tool=~"$tool"}[$__rate_interval])), 1e-9)

panels.title: Latency  ·  requires an OpenTelemetry SDK — see panel descriptions
Operation duration distribution
panels.description:
EMPTY UNLESS AN OTEL SDK IS REGISTERED, and that is by design.

cyberchef-mcp depends on `@opentelemetry/api` and nothing else -- 1 package, 2.6 MB, +9 ms startup -- rather than the SDK, which measured 71 packages, 50 MB and +100 ms. v2.6.0 spent a whole release getting cold start to 185 ms; handing half of that back on every stdio launch, for users collecting nothing, was not a trade worth making.

The server creates the spans and records this histogram; the operator supplies the SDK and picks the exporter, which means EVERY OTLP backend works rather than a chosen few:

    node --import ./otel-bootstrap.mjs src/node/mcp-server.mjs

With no SDK the instrumentation is a genuine no-op -- measured at 0.08 microseconds per span+metric cycle -- and this panel reads No data. Every other panel on this dashboard works without it.

A heatmap rather than percentile lines, because CyberChef latency is genuinely MULTI-MODAL: a cache hit, a base64 decode and a bcrypt comparison are three different populations sharing one histogram. A p95 line averages those into a number that describes none of them; the heatmap shows the bands separately, so a second band appearing is legible as a new population rather than as noise on a percentile.

Magenta dots are exemplars: click one to open the trace for that exact request. This needs `exemplarTraceIdDestinations` on the Prometheus data source -- see deploy/grafana/README.md.

panels.title: Duration percentiles
panels.description:
EMPTY UNLESS AN OTEL SDK IS REGISTERED, and that is by design.

cyberchef-mcp depends on `@opentelemetry/api` and nothing else -- 1 package, 2.6 MB, +9 ms startup -- rather than the SDK, which measured 71 packages, 50 MB and +100 ms. v2.6.0 spent a whole release getting cold start to 185 ms; handing half of that back on every stdio launch, for users collecting nothing, was not a trade worth making.

The server creates the spans and records this histogram; the operator supplies the SDK and picks the exporter, which means EVERY OTLP backend works rather than a chosen few:

    node --import ./otel-bootstrap.mjs src/node/mcp-server.mjs

With no SDK the instrumentation is a genuine no-op -- measured at 0.08 microseconds per span+metric cycle -- and this panel reads No data. Every other panel on this dashboard works without it.

Series: `mcp.server.operation.duration` from the MCP OpenTelemetry semantic conventions, recorded in SECONDS as the convention specifies (not milliseconds -- recording ms under a seconds-typed instrument is the kind of error that produces a dashboard wrong by three orders of magnitude that nobody notices).

Read alongside the heatmap: percentiles are the right thing to ALERT on, the distribution is the right thing to diagnose from.

panels.title: Errors by type
panels.description:
EMPTY UNLESS AN OTEL SDK IS REGISTERED, and that is by design.

cyberchef-mcp depends on `@opentelemetry/api` and nothing else -- 1 package, 2.6 MB, +9 ms startup -- rather than the SDK, which measured 71 packages, 50 MB and +100 ms. v2.6.0 spent a whole release getting cold start to 185 ms; handing half of that back on every stdio launch, for users collecting nothing, was not a trade worth making.

The server creates the spans and records this histogram; the operator supplies the SDK and picks the exporter, which means EVERY OTLP backend works rather than a chosen few:

    node --import ./otel-bootstrap.mjs src/node/mcp-server.mjs

With no SDK the instrumentation is a genuine no-op -- measured at 0.08 microseconds per span+metric cycle -- and this panel reads No data. Every other panel on this dashboard works without it.

`error.type` from the semantic conventions, which this server sets from the structured error CODE or the exception class -- never from the message.

That is not general caution: the arguments to a CyberChef tool ARE the sensitive material, and error messages quote their input. A code enum can be published to a tracing backend with different retention and different access control; a message cannot.

panels.title: Throughput by MCP method
panels.description:
EMPTY UNLESS AN OTEL SDK IS REGISTERED, and that is by design.

cyberchef-mcp depends on `@opentelemetry/api` and nothing else -- 1 package, 2.6 MB, +9 ms startup -- rather than the SDK, which measured 71 packages, 50 MB and +100 ms. v2.6.0 spent a whole release getting cold start to 185 ms; handing half of that back on every stdio launch, for users collecting nothing, was not a trade worth making.

The server creates the spans and records this histogram; the operator supplies the SDK and picks the exporter, which means EVERY OTLP backend works rather than a chosen few:

    node --import ./otel-bootstrap.mjs src/node/mcp-server.mjs

With no SDK the instrumentation is a genuine no-op -- measured at 0.08 microseconds per span+metric cycle -- and this panel reads No data. Every other panel on this dashboard works without it.

`mcp.method.name` -- `tools/call` against `tools/list`, `resources/read` and the rest. A client that re-lists tools on every request shows up here as `tools/list` tracking `tools/call` one-for-one, which is worth knowing: the tool payload is the single largest thing this server sends.

panels.title: Concurrent operations vs limit
panels.description:
The limit is PER TENANT, so the in-flight total can legitimately exceed it when several tenants are busy -- read it against Active tenants beside this panel. One tenant cannot exhaust the pool for the others; that was the point of making the quota per-tenant.

In-flight pinned at the limit with a FLAT call rate means callers are being refused.

panels.title: Active tenants
panels.description:
Tenants with at least one operation in flight.

Deliberately a COUNT and never names. A tenant identifier in a metric label is the classic way tenant identity leaks into a system nobody access-controlled for it, and label cardinality makes that permanent -- `/metrics` is unauthenticated. Per-tenant attribution comes from the audit log, which is access-controlled.

panels.title: Rate limiter
panels.description:
Callers tracked by the rate limiter, and whether it is enforcing.

`enabled` at 0 while tracked callers climb means the limiter is counting but not enforcing. Worth watching: through v2.4.x the limiter was keyed on a per-request UUID, so every call looked like a first-time caller and NOTHING was ever limited -- measured at 0 denials in 1000 requests against a limit of 5. It is keyed on the caller now.

panels.title: Cache utilisation
panels.description:
Bytes held against the configured ceiling.

Sustained at 100% with a FALLING hit ratio means the working set no longer fits and entries are being evicted before they are reused -- raise `CYBERCHEF_CACHE_MAX_SIZE`, or accept the miss rate. Sustained at 100% with a healthy hit ratio is a cache doing its job.

panels.title: Cache size
panels.description: Bytes and entry count together. The cache is per-process, so each replica warms its own and a rollout resets both to zero -- a sawtooth aligned with the restart annotations is a deploy, not a leak.

panels.title: Data throughput
panels.description: Bytes in and out of operations. A caller pushing large payloads shows here before the memory panel reacts to it, which is usually enough warning to act on.

panels.title: Memory per replica
panels.description:
RSS and heap.

EXPECT A STEP of roughly 100-200 MB the first time `cyberchef_search`, batch search or a saved recipe runs on a given replica. That is the Node API loading all 505 operation implementations -- deferred in v2.6.0 to take cold start from ~1300 ms to ~185 ms. It happens once per process and is NOT a leak.

A container memory limit below that step will OOM at that moment rather than at startup, which is a confusing place to find out. The chart's `resources.requests.memory` default of 256Mi and limit of 1Gi are sized for it.

panels.title: Uptime per replica
panels.description:
A sawtooth is a restart loop. Purple annotations mark each restart; correlate a drop against the Draining panel at the top to distinguish a planned roll from a crash.

Restarts derived with `resets()`, which is exact here: uptime rises monotonically within a process and can only fall by the process being replaced.

panels.title: Telemetry buffer
panels.description:
Per-call telemetry records currently held in memory.

0 on a default deployment, and that is correct: `CYBERCHEF_TELEMETRY_ENABLED` is off by default and gates the per-call records -- durations, sizes, timestamps, one row per execution. It does NOT gate the tool counters every other panel here is built on, so an empty buffer is not an empty dashboard.

The buffer is a 10,000-entry ring. Sitting at 10,000 means it is rolling over and `cyberchef_telemetry_export` returns a window, not a history.

list.description: Filters the tool panels. Sourced from tool_calls_total, so only tools that have actually been called appear -- with 300+ registered tools a list of every possible name would be unusable, and would be almost entirely names nobody has invoked.
